name: Ivan Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the late shift at a 24-hour supermarket on the ring road, two till to midnight, sometimes through to six when someone drops out. Early on it's tills and the after-work rush, then from about nine it's replenishment, cages of stock, and keeping an eye on the self-checkouts. I like the quiet hour around one in the morning when the shelves are full and it looks right. What wears me out is the shift pattern, because I see my girlfriend Lena mostly as she's leaving for her care job.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any technology in the job beyond the tills?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The handheld gun for stock counts, and the store app that tells me what's short. Now and then I use an AI chat thing on my phone to tidy up the handover notes for the morning manager, because my writing's not great when I'm tired. I didn't trust it at first, but my mate on days used it for months, so I tried it. It's useful, not magic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit. Everyone said AI would run the shop, and here we are still stacking beans by hand. At work I'd joke that the robot uprising got stuck at the bagging area.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means more of the same, and the same isn't great. I'm on lower pay than the big chains nearby, and Lena and I have maybe three weeks of money saved. The job's safe enough, but the rent and the car eat everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on nights, because the night premium is what keeps us afloat. I'd try to get Lena's and my savings up to two months by cutting the second car we barely use. Maybe I'd go for the store manager course the company runs, since nothing else is shifting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than scared. It's a grey kind of feeling, like a long winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a second car. Whose is it, and what would selling it change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's Lena's old hatchback, which she uses when our shifts clash. If we sold it, that's maybe two thousand in the bank and no insurance to pay. We'd have to juggle lifts, but it would be the first real cushion we've had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the self-checkouts? Would they keep spreading in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd keep creeping, same as now, maybe two more a year. Self-checkouts creeping in isn't AI, it's just the company counting heads. I'd still be the one resetting them at midnight.

say: I'd joke that the **robot uprising** got stuck at the **bagging area**.
Everyone said AI would run the shop, and we're still **stacking shelves** by hand.
think: My job looks **safe enough**, but **lower pay** keeps life tight.
We have about **three weeks** saved, and rent and the **car** eat everything.
do: Stay on **nights** for the premium that keeps the household afloat.
Sell **Lena's hatchback** to build a cushion of about **£2,000**.
Apply for the company's **store manager course** while things stay steady.
feel: **Uneasy**, a grey feeling like a **long winter** rather than fear.
S0.quote: Self-checkouts creeping in isn't AI, it's just the company counting heads.
fieldNote: He separates **ordinary cost-cutting** from AI and sees self-checkouts as the former.
Money is the **real pressure**, with three weeks saved and a car to run.
Selling the second car is a **practical, proven** step, true to his style.
He'd climb the **company ladder** when the ground is still.

steps.text: Keep working the late shift for the night premium
Sell Lena's old hatchback and bank about £2,000
Sign up for the company's store manager course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the union needs to be at the table before the software arrives, not after. I'd post about it, because I've seen how the self-checkouts came in with no talk at all. If the company saves money, some of it should come back as training and hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the night shift is where they test robots first, because there are no customers to complain. My job is mostly hands-on, so I've got a few years, but the stock ordering I do on the app will be all automatic soon. That leaves me as a shelf stacker with a supervisor's title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Marek, the fridge engineer who comes in every month, about how he got into refrigeration. I'd look at a part-time course in it, because cold rooms and freezers need people who can fix them. And I'd learn the store's new software inside out, so I'm the one they ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a direction. Like I can see a door, just not how far away it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why refrigeration in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every shop, hospital and restaurant has fridges, and when one breaks at three in the morning, it's thousands in stock gone. Marek charges like a dentist and he's booked out for weeks. A robot that stacks shelves is one thing, but fixing a compressor in a cramped back room is another.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for a course on your wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carefully. There's a college course for about eight hundred, paid monthly, and the union sometimes helps with fees. I'd use the money from selling Lena's car, which hurts, because that was meant to be our cushion.

say: The **union** must be at the table **before** the software arrives.
Some of the company's **savings** should come back as **training** and hours.
think: The **night shift** is where they'll test **robots** first, with no customers watching.
Automatic **stock ordering** would leave me a shelf stacker with a **supervisor's title**.
do: Ask the **fridge engineer** how he got into **refrigeration** work.
Pay for a **part-time course** of about £800 in monthly instalments.
Learn the store's **new software** so I'm the one people ask.
feel: **Anxious**, but he can see a **door** out, just not how far.
S1.quote: A robot that stacks shelves is one thing, but fixing a compressor in a cramped back room is another.
fieldNote: He reasons about **which hands-on work** stays human longest, not just which jobs go.
Willing to spend his only **cushion** on a course, a real trade-off.
Wants the **union** involved early, after seeing self-checkouts imposed.
Treats the ordering software as something to **master**, not fear.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time refrigeration course at about £800
Master the store's new automatic ordering software
Ask the union to negotiate training before new software arrives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs governments to step in now, like with the banks in a crisis. Support for people who lose work, and limits on how fast firms can lay off. I'd be sharing that everywhere and I'd vote for whoever said it clearly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think I'd be finished at the supermarket by 2031 or so. The 2028 part takes the ordering and the rota off me, then three years later the robots come for the shelves and tills. Even refrigeration gets robots eventually, so I'd only be buying time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the refrigeration course straight away, nights and weekends, no waiting. We'd cut everything: no holiday, no eating out, sell the second car. And I'd ask my parents whether we could live with them for a while if it came to that, which I've never wanted to ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the floor's been pulled out and I'm still standing on it out of habit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Lena's job look like in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Care work is hands-on, so she'd have a few more years, maybe more because families want a person. But the agency she works for already cuts her travel time to the minute with an app. If they get smarter software, she gets squeezed harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said even refrigeration gets robots eventually. Why do it, then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buying time is still worth something, because doing nothing just means I'm broke sooner. If I get five or six years of decent pay as an engineer, that's money in the bank before whatever comes after.

say: Governments must **step in now**, like they did for the **banks**.
I'd vote for whoever promises **support** and slower **layoffs** clearly.
think: I'd be **finished** at the supermarket by about **2031**.
Even **refrigeration** gets robots eventually, so retraining only **buys time**.
do: Start the **refrigeration course** immediately on nights and weekends.
Cancel the **holiday**, stop eating out and sell the second car.
Ask my **parents** whether we could move in with them for a while.
feel: **Alarmed**, like the floor's gone and he's standing there **out of habit**.
S2.quote: Buying time is still worth something, because doing nothing just means I'm broke sooner.
fieldNote: He sees the **three-year robot gap** as a window to earn, not to wait.
Asking his parents for help is a **line** he never wanted to cross.
Worries for his partner's **care job** being squeezed by smarter scheduling.
Clear-eyed that retraining is a **delay**, not a rescue.

steps.text: Start the refrigeration course at once on nights and weekends
Cancel this year's holiday and stop eating out
Ask his parents about moving in if the job goes
Vote for candidates promising limits on fast layoffs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan if people start now, so the union and the council should start now. Retraining money, help with fees, honest dates from employers. I'd say that at the branch meeting and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years feels like just enough for me. I could finish a refrigeration qualification in two years and get a few years in before robots get good at the tills in 2034. It's tight, but it's a plan, and I like having one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the course over two years instead of cramming it, and keep my supermarket job while I do. I'd put my overtime money aside for the tools, which are about fifteen hundred. And I'd keep using the AI stuff at work, so I'm not starting cold when it gets serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but steadier. Like a long walk home in the rain rather than a sprint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'a few years in' as an engineer. What then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. Maybe by then there's new work fixing the robots themselves, maybe there isn't. I'd rather be someone with a trade and some savings when that question comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Lena change any plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about getting married in two years, maybe a small do. We'd still do it, just smaller, at her aunt's garden rather than a hall. Kids we'd keep putting off until I've got the new job.

say: Five years is **enough to plan**, so the union and council should start now.
People need **retraining money**, help with fees and **honest dates**.
think: Five years feels **just enough** to qualify and work before **2034**.
It's **tight**, but having a plan makes me feel better.
do: Spread the **refrigeration qualification** over two years while keeping the supermarket job.
Keep using **AI tools** at work so I'm not starting cold.
feel: **Anxious** but steadier, like a long walk home in the **rain**.
S3.quote: I'd rather be someone with a trade and some savings when that question comes.
fieldNote: Five years matches his **pace**: steady, step by step, with proof along the way.
He admits he **doesn't know** what comes after the robots arrive.
**Wedding plans** shrink rather than vanish; children are pushed back.
Keeps the day job as a **safety net** while training.

steps.text: Take the refrigeration qualification over two years part-time
Save overtime pay towards £1,500 of engineer's tools
Keep using the AI note tool for night handovers
Hold a smaller wedding at Lena's aunt's garden

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so don't waste it arguing about whether it's real. I'd be pushing the union to set up proper training with the company, paid for, over years. On social media I'd keep it simple: plan now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years makes me relax a bit, maybe too much. Robots good enough for the tills by 2039 means I'm nearly forty before the shop floor really goes. I'd probably carry on for a couple of years and see how fast things move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay put for the first year or two and watch what the company does with the new systems. I'd get the store manager course done, because that pays more meanwhile. Then around 2029, if things look real, I'd start refrigeration properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not tight in the chest. It feels like there's room to breathe and think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years might make you relax too much. What worries you about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'll be thirty-five and still on nights, telling myself there's time. My dad did that with his factory job and ended up on the sorting line at fifty-three. I don't want to be his story again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would tell you it's time to stop watching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the company stops hiring for nights. If the supermarket doesn't replace people who leave the night shift, that's the robots getting closer, whatever head office says.

say: Ten years is a **gift**, so stop arguing about whether it's **real**.
I'd push for **paid training** with the company spread over years.
think: Ten years makes me **relax**, maybe more than I should.
The **shop floor** really goes around **2039**, when I'm nearly forty.
do: Watch the company's **new systems** for a year or two before deciding.
Finish the **store manager course** to earn more in the meantime.
Start **refrigeration** properly around **2029** if the change looks real.
S4.quote: If the supermarket doesn't replace people who leave the night shift, that's the robots getting closer, whatever head office says.
fieldNote: The long warning makes him **wait**, and he knows that's a risk.
His **father's factory story** is the warning he carries.
He has a clear **trigger**: no new hires on nights.
Still expects his income to shift, so the worry stays real.

steps.text: Watch whether the store stops hiring for the night shift
Finish the company's store manager course for higher pay
Ask the union to agree paid multi-year training with the company

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because there's no time to train for anything before the shelves go. What would help is a course I can afford, ideally paid for, and the company being honest about when. Also something for Lena, because care workers get forgotten in all this.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about nights. When the robots come, it's night-shift students, carers and people with second jobs who lose the one shift that fits their life. Nobody's talking about them.

headlineQuote: When the robots come, it's night-shift students, carers and people with second jobs who lose the one shift that fits their life.
portrait: Ivan is a **27-year-old** late-shift supervisor at a 24-hour ring-road supermarket, on lower pay.
He and his partner Lena, a **care worker**, have about three weeks of savings.
He's **steady**: he uses AI for handover notes after watching a colleague try it first.
His plan across the AGI pictures is **refrigeration engineering**, which he sees as buying time.
He moves from uneasy in **AI Plateau** to alarmed with only two years' warning.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the shelves go before he can **train** for anything.
whatWouldHelp: An **affordable course** and honest **dates** from the company.
Support for **care workers** like his partner, who he feels get forgotten.
